title: 02 — Lazy Queries and the Optimiser
html:
02 — Lazy Queries and the Optimiser

The one idea: a LazyFrame is a plan, not data. Scanning lazily lets Polars push filters and column choices into the file reader, run shared work once, and (since Polars 2) stream batches through every core. The price is that results that don't ask for an order don't promise one.

1. What it is

Term Meaning
scan_parquet / scan_csv / scan_ipc Start a lazy plan from files. Nothing is read yet
read_* Read the whole file now (eager). Since Polars 2, read_csv and read_ipc are implemented as scan_*(...).collect() internally
collect() Optimise the plan and run it
explain() Print the optimised plan
Predicate pushdown Filters move into the reader, which skips row groups whose statistics can't match
Projection pushdown Only the needed columns leave the disk
Slice pushdown head(n) stops reading early
Common subplan elimination A shared part of several queries runs once (with collect_all)
Engine "auto" (default), "streaming", "in-memory", "gpu". In Polars 2, "auto" means streaming for lazy queries 
---
title: From a lazy query to a result
---
flowchart LR
    Q["LazyFrame plan"] --> O["Optimiser<br/>pushdowns, simplify, CSE"]
    O --> E["Streaming engine<br/>(default since 2.0)"]
    E --> R1["collect() → DataFrame"]
    E --> R2["sink_parquet() → file"]
    E --> R3["collect_batches() → chunks"]

2. Why it matters

  • Reading 10% of a file instead of 100% is often the single biggest speed-up.
  • Plans can be inspected, so you can see why a query is slow before running it.
  • The Polars 2 default changed results that relied on incidental row order. Code that worked on 1.x can now return rows in a different order.

3. The main ideas

3.1 Scan, then filter and select early

Write the filters and the column list as if the whole file were loaded. The optimiser moves them into the scan. Sorting files by a common filter column (dates) makes row-group statistics far more useful.

3.2 Read the plan

In explain() output, look under the scan for PROJECT k/n COLUMNS (projection pushdown) and SELECTION: (predicate pushdown). If your filter sits above the scan instead, something blocked the pushdown, often a Python function in the filter.

3.3 Branching plans run twice unless you say otherwise

A LazyFrame held in a variable is a recipe. Two collect() calls on two branches compute the shared base twice. pl.collect_all([q1, q2]) (or several sinks with lazy=True) runs them as one plan with the shared part cached.

3.4 Polars 2: streaming by default, order not guaranteed

Change in 2.0 What to do
collect() on a lazy query uses the streaming engine Usually faster. Nothing to do
Streaming doesn't keep row order for joins, group_by, unpivot unless asked join(..., maintain_order="left"), group_by(..., maintain_order=True), or sort before you rely on order
LazyFrame.profile() removed Time whole queries, read explain(), or use Polars' query monitoring
Restore the old engine pl.Config.set_engine_affinity("in-memory"), collect(engine="in-memory"), or POLARS_ENGINE_AFFINITY=in-memory

4. Working code

The script writes 5 million NAV rows sorted by date, then compares eager and lazy reads, prints a plan, compares two collects with collect_all, and shows the row-order change in joins.

import os, time
import polars as pl

os.makedirs("data", exist_ok=True)
n = 5_000_000
(
    pl.LazyFrame({"id": pl.int_range(n, eager=True)})
    .with_columns(
        (pl.col("id") % 50).alias("fund"),
        pl.date(2026, 1, 1).dt.offset_by(pl.format("{}d", pl.col("id") % 300)).alias("nav_date"),
        ((pl.col("id") * 7919 % 100_000) / 100).alias("nav"),
        pl.format("note-{}", pl.col("id") % 977).alias("comment"),
    )
    .sort("nav_date")                       # sorted dates make row-group statistics useful
    .sink_parquet("data/navs.parquet", row_group_size=250_000)
)
print("file size:", round(os.path.getsize("data/navs.parquet") / 1e6, 1), "MB")

def timed(label, fn, runs=3):
    best = float("inf")
    for _ in range(runs):                    # best of three, so file caching favours neither side
        t = time.perf_counter(); out = fn(); best = min(best, time.perf_counter() - t)
    print(f"{label:<50} {best:6.3f} s  rows={out.height}")
    return out

eager = timed("eager: read everything, then filter",
              lambda: pl.read_parquet("data/navs.parquet")
                       .filter(pl.col("nav_date") >= pl.date(2026, 10, 1))
                       .select("fund", "nav"))
lazy = timed("lazy: scan with predicate + projection pushdown",
             lambda: pl.scan_parquet("data/navs.parquet")
                      .filter(pl.col("nav_date") >= pl.date(2026, 10, 1))
                      .select("fund", "nav").collect())
assert eager.sort(pl.all()).equals(lazy.sort(pl.all()))

q = (pl.scan_parquet("data/navs.parquet")
     .filter(pl.col("fund") == 7)
     .group_by("nav_date").agg(pl.col("nav").mean()))
print("\n--- optimised plan ---")
print(q.explain())

# Two results from one expensive base: collect_all runs the shared part once.
base = pl.scan_parquet("data/navs.parquet").with_columns((pl.col("nav") * 1.01).alias("adj"))
by_fund = base.group_by("fund").agg(pl.col("adj").sum())
by_date = base.group_by("nav_date").agg(pl.col("adj").max())
def best(fn, runs=3):
    out = float("inf")
    for _ in range(runs):
        t = time.perf_counter(); fn(); out = min(out, time.perf_counter() - t)
    return out
separate = best(lambda: (by_fund.collect(), by_date.collect()))
together = best(lambda: pl.collect_all([by_fund, by_date]))
print(f"\ntwo collects: {separate:.3f} s   collect_all: {together:.3f} s")

# Polars 2: lazy queries default to the streaming engine, which does not promise row order.
left = pl.LazyFrame({"k": list(range(200_000))})
right = pl.LazyFrame({"k": list(range(200_000))[::-1], "v": list(range(200_000))})
joined = left.join(right, on="k", how="left").collect()
kept = left.join(right, on="k", how="left", maintain_order="left").collect()
print("left order kept without maintain_order:", joined["k"].equals(left.collect()["k"]))
print("left order kept with maintain_order='left':", kept["k"].equals(left.collect()["k"]))

Output:

file size: 6.8 MB
eager: read everything, then filter                 0.027 s  rows=449982
lazy: scan with predicate + projection pushdown     0.003 s  rows=449982

--- optimised plan ---
AGGREGATE[maintain_order: false]
  [col("nav").mean()] BY [col("nav_date")]
  FROM
  simple π 2/2 ["nav_date", "nav"]
    Parquet SCAN [data/navs.parquet]
    PROJECT 3/5 COLUMNS
    SELECTION: col("fund") == 7
    ESTIMATED ROWS: 5000000

two collects: 0.041 s   collect_all: 0.045 s
left order kept without maintain_order: False
left order kept with maintain_order='left': True

What to notice:

  • The lazy query was about 9× faster for the same 449,982 rows. It read 2 of 5 columns, and skipped every row group before October using the date statistics.
  • The plan shows both pushdowns under the scan: PROJECT 3/5 COLUMNS and SELECTION: col("fund") == 7.
  • collect_all beat two separate collects because the shared scan ran once. The gain grows with how expensive the shared part is.
  • Without maintain_order, the left join came back in a different order. On Polars 1.x it usually matched the left side, so code silently depended on it.

5. Common mistakes

  1. read_parquet(...).filter(...) when scan_parquet(...).filter(...).collect() would read a fraction.
  2. Collecting in the middle of a pipeline to "check something", which breaks the plan in two.
  3. Reusing a lazy variable in several collects and paying for it each time.
  4. Relying on row order after a join or group_by without asking for it.
  5. Python functions inside filters, which block predicate pushdown.

6. Exercise (1 hour)

  1. Remove the .sort("nav_date") before writing, and rerun the eager vs lazy comparison. Explain the change.
  2. Print explain() for a query with .head(10) and find the slice pushdown.
  3. Add a third branch to the collect_all example and compare again.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. What is the difference between scan_parquet and read_parquet?
  2. Where in explain() output do you see predicate pushdown?
  3. Why can two collect() calls on related queries be slower than collect_all?
  4. What changed about collect() in Polars 2?
  5. How do you keep the left-hand row order in a join?

Answers

  1. scan_parquet builds a lazy plan the optimiser can push work into. read_parquet reads the file now.
  2. As SELECTION: under the scan node.
  3. Each collect runs the shared base again. collect_all runs it once.
  4. For lazy queries, the default engine is now streaming, which doesn't guarantee row order where the operation doesn't need it.
  5. join(..., maintain_order="left").

8. Sources
